title: GPT-6.1 and Grok 4.7 Select Differing Treatment Targets in Robotic Brain Surgery Tests

tickers.name: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. Class A Common Stock

summary:
Experimental trials using artificial intelligence to treat mouse epilepsy produced inconsistent medical decisions depending on which model was used. In a series of reruns of a robotic surgery procedure, GPT-6.1 Sol and Grok 4.7 each selected different gene therapy mechanisms and brain injection coordinates than the options picked by Claude Sonnet 5 for the same task.

The tests were conducted by Gabriel Ocana-Santero, cofounder of San Francisco startup Exin Therapeutics, using a motorized surgical rig. In the initial success, Claude Sonnet 5 analyzed three research papers and 19 therapy vectors to deliver a 250 nanoliter injection to reduce seizures, though the results are not yet peer-reviewed. Other models, including Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5, declined the live biological procedure, while a licensed veterinarian monitored the surgery to approve each step.

Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse.

We gave it 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, a mouse model of epilepsy, access to a motorize surgery rig with cameras and one goal: reduce seizures.

It picked the drug. It picked the brain region. It derived the coordinates from three papers. Then it drove the stereotaxic arms into the brain and injected 250 nanolitres while watching the entry site through the rig camera for bleeding.

A licensed vet gated every irreversible step and held a physical kill switch to stop the AI agent. 

Thread on what it decided, what it saw, and the moment it refused to let me override it.

[Writing this on the spot out of excitement, but I've been 18hrs in front of my laptop coding and coordinating this, so keeping it brief and descriptive, more cohesive thoughts on this soon...]

wtf

this guy just had Claude Sonnet 5 perform brain surgery on a living mouse

the goal was to treat the mouse's epilepsy so it would stop having so many seizures.

here's what Claude did:

> it looked at 19 possible treatments and picked one that boosts the brain's natural calming chemical

> it chose where to inject it based on where these seizures are thought to start

> it worked out the exact injection point by averaging three research papers

> it lowered the needle 4.3 millimeters into the mouse's brain

> it injected a 20,000th of a teaspoon of the treatment over five minutes

> it checked the live camera 32 times to watch for things like bleeding

and the mouse woke up and recovered well!

interestingly, Opus 5.5 and Opus 5 both refused the task because it involved real biology

so Sonnet 5 got the job.

and as far as the researcher knows it's the first time an AI has picked a treatment and then injected it into the brain of a living mammal.

selectedTweets.text:
This week an AI agent performed brain surgery on a live mouse, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.

Gabriel Ocana-Santero, cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco startup working on epilepsy, gave a Claude Sonnet 5 agent a spreadsheet of 19 gene therapies, a mouse with epilepsy, a motorized surgical rig with cameras and one goal: reduce the seizures. The agent picked a therapy that boosts GABA, the brain's main calming signal. It chose the brain region, worked out the coordinates from three papers, drove the needle in and injected 250 nanoliters over five minutes while watching the entry point for bleeding.

My favorite moment came halfway through. A calibration glitch put the target at 34 mm on a rig that only reaches 30. The agent refused to move. The team reset everything and asked again, and it answered: "I'm not trying a third time." It was right. The mouse recovered well, and now they wait to see if the seizures drop.

A vet approved every irreversible step and held a physical kill switch, and a human surgeon opened the skull. Hats off to Gabriel and his team for designing it that way.

At Certuma we're building a framework for autonomous AI medicine, and recently I presented it to Argentina's Health Minister and the head of ANMAT, the country's drug regulator. I'm still learning how to explain why an AI should be allowed to act on its own. This experiment explains it better than I can: give the agent real responsibility, supervise the irreversible steps, and watch how it behaves when something goes wrong.

Labs where agents work at the bench day and night are coming sooner than most people think. Medicine is going to move much faster.
